Export Industry ESG Assessment & BRSR Reporting Framework

A structured ESG assessment, KPI, benchmarking and BRSR-aligned reporting framework for the Indian export industry — integrating environmental, social and governance indicators with BRSR principles, operational evidence, industry benchmarks, stakeholder expectations and a weighted scoring methodology.

Project overview

India's export industry does not operate as a single entity. It is a highly integrated value chain that links farms, manufacturing factories, suppliers, service providers, logistics providers, ports, freight forwarders, customs teams and overseas buyers — and the architecture of that ecosystem is what makes ESG assessment difficult. Because the sector operates at scale across numerous sites and suppliers, even minor fluctuations in operational performance can materially affect lead times, costs and reputational exposure.

The consequence for assessment is direct: an accurate industry profile has to look beyond the factory gate to take in logistics corridors, outsourced operations and buyer-mandated requirements. Issues such as sustainability or quality do not stay inside one department. They land simultaneously on procurement, operations, logistics, finance and buyer confidence.

The economic scale sets the stakes. Official government trade reporting places merchandise exports at US$ 437.07 billion during 2023-24, with services exports of US$ 341.06 billion; the latest government estimates for April–February 2025-26 put total exports at US$ 790.86 billion. Merchandise exports grew from US$ 310.34 billion in 2014-15 to US$ 437.07 billion in 2023-24, against imports of US$ 678.21 billion in that year. The sector is inherently cyclical, driven by global demand, fuel prices and shifting freight conditions — which is why its performance is better measured through operational intensity, resilience and value addition than through absolute growth figures alone.

Fiscal yearExports (US$ bn)Imports (US$ bn)

2021-22422613
2023-24437678

International trade data as charted in the assessment document. The gap between the two series is the structural feature worth noting: imports have grown faster in absolute terms across the decade, which is part of why export performance is read through intensity and resilience rather than headline growth.

This project develops a structured ESG assessment and reporting framework for that context. It integrates environmental, social and governance indicators with the BRSR principles, operational evidence, industry benchmark reference points, stakeholder expectations and a weighted scoring methodology — so that ESG performance can be evaluated, documented and communicated across the value chain rather than asserted at the level of a single site.

Why ESG matters in export businesses

The argument is not that ESG is important. It is that ESG performance is already operating on the commercial variables an exporter is judged on.

Environmental performance

Energy consumption, emissions, water usage, wastewater, waste recovery and environmental controls influence operating costs, buyer expectations and compliance exposure.

Social performance

Worker safety, workforce structure, training, fair treatment, grievances and human rights affect workforce resilience and buyer confidence.

Governance

Ethics, compliance, board oversight, supplier controls and data management determine transparency and organisational accountability.

Supply chain

ESG risks may sit well beyond the factory, which is what makes supplier mapping, audits and traceability part of the assessment rather than an add-on.

Market access

Global buyers increasingly expect credible sustainability evidence — not a statement of intent, but something that survives a scorecard.

Business resilience

Climate events, logistics disruptions, regulatory requirements and supply-chain weaknesses can interrupt export continuity and delivery performance.

Export industry ecosystem & value chain

ESG data and risk information have to move along the same path as the physical goods. Each stage generates evidence, and each hand-off is a point where traceability is either preserved or lost.

  1. 01Raw material / farms
  2. 02Suppliers
  3. 03Manufacturing
  4. 04Quality & compliance
  5. 05Logistics
  6. 06Ports / customs
  7. 07International buyers
  8. 08Markets / customers

ESG cannot be assessed only at factory level. Because the ecosystem spans many sites and suppliers, the assessment boundary has to include logistics corridors, outsourced operations and buyer-mandated requirements.

Key ESG hotspots by export cluster

Each product cluster carries a distinct risk profile, which changes what the reporting has to emphasise.

Textiles & apparel

Water • chemicals • labour • energy. High exposure to water use, chemical handling and labour-intensive processes. Reporting emphasis falls on dyeing controls, effluent, traceability and worker welfare.

Engineering goods

Energy • scrap • machining waste • safety. Operations heavy in energy use and scrap generation, with controls emphasising energy efficiency, metal recovery and machine guarding.

Electronics

Hazardous waste • data • supplier traceability. Risks around e-waste, data security and supplier traceability, requiring cyber controls and supplier mapping.

Food & agro exports

Water • cold chain • hygiene • loss control. Vulnerabilities around water consumption, cold chain integrity and hygiene, placing a premium on food safety and recall readiness.

Gems, jewellery & leather

Origin • ethics • chemical use • labour. Stakeholders scrutinise origin, chemical use and ethics, requiring due diligence, responsible sourcing and proof of authenticity.

BRSR-aligned ESG framework

The framework is applied through two structural components: the nine BRSR principles as the qualitative foundation, and BRSR Core as the measurable component. The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting framework mandates reporting across nine principles for SEBI-listed entities, and it maps closely onto the operational realities of an export business.

P1

Ethics, transparency & accountability

Board conduct, ethics training, and the tracking of compliance issues, fines and penalties.

P2

Sustainable goods & services

Eco-design, product safety, Extended Producer Responsibility and sustainable sourcing.

P3

Employee well-being & value chain labour

Workplace safety, insurance access, fair wages and harassment prevention — across the value chain, not only in-house.

P4

Stakeholder responsiveness

Structured identification, mapping and engagement of material stakeholders.

P5

Human rights

Human rights due diligence, grievance systems and remedy protocols, including value-chain risk.

P6

Environment protection & restoration

Energy, water, waste and emissions tracking, supported by an environmental management system.

P7

Responsible policy engagement

Transparent disclosure of trade association memberships and public advocacy positions.

P8

Inclusive growth & equitable development

Community impact, local development programmes and Social Impact Assessment.

P9

Customer value & responsibility

Truthful labelling, rigorous quality and safety controls, and data protection.

From narrative ESG to measurable ESG

The nine principles guide the narrative. BRSR Core narrows the spotlight to strict, quantifiable indicators — SEBI's guidance expects these disclosures to be comparable, evidence-based and useful to investors and stakeholders. Under BRSR Core, export companies are asked to quantify hard metrics rather than describe intentions.

Applying the framework also means stating the reporting boundary explicitly — whether the report covers a stand-alone entity or consolidated operations, and how it treats value-chain data. A disclosure is only as strong as its evidence trail, so each principle has to be linked to auditable sources such as utility bills, HR logs and board minutes. That is what turns a principle into something an assurance provider can test:

  1. 01ESG principle
  2. 02Indicator
  3. 03Data source
  4. 04Responsible owner
  5. 05Management review

ESG indicator architecture

The indicator set is organised in three domains. Each indicator is defined by what it measures and why it is measured, rather than named and left to interpretation.

Environmental

Four indicator families

Energy & emissions

Energy intensity per unit output, percentage of renewable electricity, and Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions intensity measured as CO₂e per unit output.

Water stewardship

Total water consumption, water intensity per unit output, and wastewater discharge categorised by treatment level.

Waste & circularity

Percentage of waste recovered, with separate accounting for hazardous and non-hazardous streams including scrap, sludge, packaging and e-waste.

Land & biodiversity

Habitat disturbance, land conversion and stormwater handling, assessed particularly during facility expansion.

Social

Five indicator families

Workforce & diversity

Total headcount across permanent, fixed-term and contract staff, alongside female representation and pay equity.

Health & safety

Lost Time Injury Frequency Rate, total serious incidents, and direct spending on employee wellbeing.

Training & skills

Training coverage as a percentage, total training hours, and competency completion rates.

Human rights & grievances

Grievance case count and closure time, with indicators for forced labour, child labour and discrimination in the supply chain.

Customer & product responsibility

Product conformity, labelling accuracy, complaint handling and product recall readiness.

Governance

Four indicator families

Board oversight & ethics

Meeting cadence of the ESG committee, completion of ethics training, and resolution of compliance audits.

Compliance control

Logs for environmental permits, labour compliance, customs and tax obligations, so that no filing is missed.

Risk & data management

Residual risk levels, cyber security incidents, and management of sensitive customer data.

Policy engagement

Affiliations with trade associations and chambers of commerce, and official public policy positions.

ESG data collection & evidence methodology

The methodology runs in four stages, and its purpose is to make the eventual disclosure defensible rather than merely complete.

  • STAGE 1
    External context data
    Trade, labour and demographic context from official Indian sources — Ministry of Commerce trade releases, MOSPI labour and population statistics, and SEBI's BRSR format and BRSR Core circular.
  • STAGE 2
    Internal operational evidence
    To remain audit-ready for limited assurance, primary source evidence is retained rather than narrative summaries: meter logs, utility invoices, site registers, training sheets, grievance logs and supplier questionnaires.
  • STAGE 3
    System integration
    Collection is integrated into single dashboards that reconcile bills, meter data, production volumes and improvement initiatives. Supplier audits collect data on labour standards, environmental controls and origin documentation.
  • STAGE 4
    Governance & accountability
    Every data point is connected to a measurable owner, a specific data source and a management review cycle.
  1. 01Bills
  2. 02Meter data
  3. 03Production
  4. 04ESG KPIs
  5. 05Improvement actions

Audit-ready ESG reporting depends on evidence, ownership and traceability.

ESG scoring model

Each operational metric is scored from 0 to 10 against industry baselines and targets.

10

Best-in-class / target exceeded

For example 100% renewable energy, or zero safety incidents.

5

Industry average / baseline met

Performance in line with the sector reference point.

0

Non-compliant / severe risk

For example major regulatory fines, or zero waste recovered.

Weighting strategy

In heavy manufacturing and export industries, environmental and supply chain impacts are the most heavily scrutinised by overseas buyers, and the weights reflect that.

Environmental40%
Energy · Water · Waste · Emissions
Social30%
Safety (LTIFR) · Training · Diversity · Grievances
Governance30%
Supplier audits · Compliance · Board oversight · Data security
Weighted score = (E × 0.40) + (S × 0.30) + (G × 0.30) Each domain scored 0–10 against baseline and target, then combined to a single score out of 10

ESG grading matrix

The final weighted score determines the grade.

8.5 – 10.0
Grade A · Export leader

Highly attractive to premium global buyers.

6.0 – 8.4
Grade B · Developing / average

Meets standard compliance, with room for operational efficiency.

Below 6.0
Grade C · High risk / laggard

Risk of losing export contracts or facing regulatory penalties.

The grading bands and their descriptions are reproduced from the source report. A grade is an assessment output, not a guarantee of any commercial outcome.

ESG management dashboard concept

This is a conceptual monitoring cycle, not a software product — no platform was built as part of this work. It describes how the framework would be operated if the indicator architecture, evidence methodology and scoring model were run together on a management cadence.

  1. Data collection — from meters, bills, registers and supplier returns
  2. KPI validation — reconciliation against production and source records
  3. ESG score — weighted across environmental, social and governance domains
  4. Risk identification — red flags where a metric breaches its threshold
  5. Corrective action — assigned to the named owner of the indicator
  6. Management review — performance, trends and target achievement
  7. Disclosure — BRSR-aligned reporting with the evidence trail attached

Red flags

Indicators breaching a threshold or moving against target are surfaced rather than averaged away in a summary.

KPI trends

Direction over time matters more than a single period, because a metric can meet target while deteriorating.

Target achievement

Progress measured against the baseline and annual target set for each indicator.

Responsible owner

Every indicator carries a named owner, which is what makes a corrective action assignable.

Corrective action

Tracked to closure rather than to acknowledgement — the same discipline audit follow-up requires.

Evidence availability

Whether the supporting record exists and is retrievable, checked before disclosure rather than during assurance.

Business implications of ESG performance

Supply chain impact

Traceability is no longer optional; it is a core expectation in export markets, particularly for textiles, food, electronics and minerals. Supply chains will have to adopt systems where origin, quality, labour and environmental data move alongside the physical goods. Exporters can no longer plead ignorance about supplier practices — supplier audits must actively cover labour standards, environmental controls and business ethics, which is likely to force consolidation of the vendor base in favour of suppliers who can provide clean, audit-ready data.

Logistics and multimodal scrutiny

Freight reliability and lead times are significant non-price competitiveness factors. Container availability, inland transport and port congestion now have to be managed not only for speed but because they directly influence reported emissions and service quality.

Revenue and market access

ESG is not only a compliance cost; it is a market opportunity. Green packaging, energy-efficient manufacturing and certified sourcing strengthen access to premium global buyers. Exporters who can prove their ESG metrics win contracts over competitors who cannot — and the operative word is prove.

Capital allocation and transition costs

The revenue model has to absorb transition risk, which arises as buyers, financiers and regulators begin demanding lower-carbon products and routes. Meeting that demand requires capital allocation to high-efficiency machinery, renewable power and advanced data analytics.

Operational resilience and compliance exposure

Physical climate risks — floods, heat, cyclones, port disruptions — interrupt export schedules directly, so disaster resilience has to be built into the revenue model to protect delivery performance. Failing to meet compliance standards can result in severe financial penalties, lost rebates or revoked customs licences.

Key insights

ESG is operational, not isolated

ESG issues do not stay within one department. They land on procurement, operations and logistics at the same time, which is why an assessment scoped to a single function will systematically understate exposure.

Traceability is becoming central to competitiveness

Origin, quality, labour and environmental data increasingly have to travel with the goods. In textiles, food, electronics and minerals this has moved from differentiator to expectation.

Supplier performance sets the ceiling on ESG credibility

An exporter cannot be more credible than its upstream evidence. Supplier audits covering labour, environment and ethics are what make a claim about the chain defensible.

Evidence matters as much as disclosure

A disclosure is only as strong as its evidence trail. Retaining meter logs, invoices, registers and grievance records is what separates audit-ready reporting from narrative reporting.

Environmental performance has direct cost implications

Energy and water are simultaneously ESG indicators and cost lines. Intensity metrics per unit output make that dual character visible in a way absolute figures do not.

Worker safety and wellbeing are measurable business indicators

LTIFR, training coverage and grievance closure are quantified operational data, not sentiment — and they behave as leading indicators of workforce resilience.

ESG data needs ownership and governance

Every data point requires a named owner, a defined source and a review cycle. Without that, the number exists but nobody can defend it under assurance.

Resilience belongs in business planning

Climate events, logistics disruption and regulatory change affect export continuity directly, which makes resilience a planning input rather than a contingency.

Case study summary

India's export industry operates as an integrated value chain linking farms, suppliers, factories, logistics providers, ports, customs and overseas buyers — which means ESG performance cannot be assessed at a single site and cannot be confined to one department. The assessment challenge is that buyers, regulators and lenders increasingly ask for evidence rather than intent, while the data needed to provide it sits scattered across meters, invoices, HR files, grievance logs and supplier returns.

This project develops a framework that closes that gap. It uses the nine BRSR principles as its qualitative foundation and BRSR Core as the measurable component, then defines an indicator architecture across environmental, social and governance domains — energy and emissions, water stewardship, waste and circularity, land and biodiversity; workforce, safety, training, human rights and product responsibility; board oversight, compliance control, risk and data management and policy engagement. A four-stage data methodology ties every indicator to a source, an owner and a review cycle, so the resulting disclosure carries an evidence trail. Industry benchmark reference points give the scoring something to score against, and a 0–10 scale weighted 40% environmental, 30% social and 30% governance produces a single grade on a three-band matrix.

The result is a practical ESG management framework rather than a theoretical discussion: it states what to measure, where the evidence comes from, who owns it, how performance is scored, and what the score implies for supply chain, market access, capital allocation and resilience.
